summary: Research how AWS/Google/Meta/Oracle/Azure architect each domain; map to Oyatie decisions

research.domain: Identity / IdP (workforce + customer identity) across AWS, Google, Meta, Microsoft Azure, Oracle OCI

per_company.approach: IAM is split into one global control plane (us-east-1) and fully independent per-region data planes spread over >=3 AZs, eventually consistent, statically stable; AWS Identity handles over half a billion authn/authz API calls per second (AWS Security Blog; re:Invent SEC404 'A day in the life of a billion requests'). Core API auth is NOT bearer tokens: every call is SigV4 request-signed with STS temporary credentials (ASIA key + secret + session token, 15min-12h, default 1h). STS temp creds are deliberately irrevocable ('bearer bonds', no phone-home per request); revocation is done by policy condition on aws:TokenIssueTime ('Revoke active sessions'). Workforce: IAM Identity Center — per-organization instance pinned to a primary region (admin functions only there), 99.95% data-plane / 99.9% control-plane design goals, SCIM provisioning, OAuth token exchange via trusted identity propagation (CreateTokenWithIAM), region replication added only recently; AWS still recommends break-glass IAM users independent of the external IdP. Customer: Cognito user pools — regional, ~50M users/pool quota, JWT access/ID tokens (default 1h, 5min-24h configurable), Managed Login + native passkeys (Nov 2024), multi-Region replication only launched June 2026 (one read-only replica). Service-to-service: IAM roles + instance-metadata-vended rotating creds everywhere, IAM Roles Anywhere (x509→STS), EKS Pod Identity; no SPIFFE internally — SigV4 is the universal service auth. Bootstrap: account root user with mandatory MFA (2024) and Nov 2024 centralized root access that programmatically deletes root credentials from member accounts.

Internal service identity is ALTS (built from 2007, whitepaper Dec 2017): mutual authn for all RPC where identity is bound to the service/role, not the host; Borg Prime issues ALTS credentials to microservices at scheduling time; end-user permission tickets (EUC) prove an RPC is on behalf of a specific user so downstream services return only that user's data (Google Infrastructure Security Design Overview). Workforce zero-trust is BeyondCorp (papers 2014-2018): access proxy + device inventory DB + trust tiers, no VPN; productized as BeyondCorp Enterprise / Context-Aware Access. Mandatory hardware security keys since ~2017: zero successful phishing across 85,000+ employees (FIDO case study). Plane separation: Cloud Identity (workforce/Workspace) vs Identity Platform (CIAM; same backend as Firebase Auth, plus multi-tenancy, SAML/OIDC, blocking functions, 99.95% SLA); Workforce/Workload Identity Federation for keyless OIDC/SAML/x509 token exchange. Passkeys at consumer scale: 400M+ accounts, >1B authentications by May 2024, passkeys used more than SMS+app OTP combined; pushing Device Bound Session Credentials (DBSC) to neutralize cookie/token theft. OAuth access tokens ~1h; sessions/cookies issued by a central identity service enabling central revocation.

Service identity = x509 certificates with the service identity in a custom X.509 extension, issued by an Internal CA when Tupperware/Twine starts the container; three cert classes (high-privilege host, identity, low-privilege host). Transport is standard TLS 1.3 via their own Fizz library (largest TLS 1.3 deployment as of 2019), with Session Ticket Encryption Keys derived per-identity KDF(ica_secret, identity) and a three-key rotation window (previous/current/next) — symmetric resumption is 'an order of magnitude' cheaper than asymmetric handshakes at thousands of services doing billions of RPS on hundreds of thousands of hosts. CATs (Crypto Auth Tokens, IACR 2018/413) are symmetric-key MAC tokens with pairwise derived secrets used for messaging backend auth, explicitly designed to avoid any online dependency or expensive crypto during disasters (availability-first auth). ACS (Anonymous Credential Service): multitenant C++ service on Twine, globally load-balanced, Thrift token issue/redeem APIs, per-use-case key material, routine key rotation via async job infra + keychain service; provides de-identified (VOPRF anonymous-credential) authentication at WhatsApp scale. Employee SSO/workforce identity is not publicly documented in comparable detail.

Entra ID Core Store is partitioned into scale units: each partition has a single highly-available primary replica taking all writes, with synchronous durable replication to a secondary in a different datacenter before ack; all reads served from geo-distributed secondary replicas; primary failover in 1-2 minutes. 99.99% authentication SLA (since 2021; April 2025 SLA calc counts backup-auth successes). The flagship resilience design is the Backup Authentication System: an independent, regionally isolated service that transparently serves authentications from cached prior policy evaluations when the primary Entra service is degraded — the IdP is engineered to survive itself. Continuous Access Evaluation (CAE, based on OpenID Shared Signals/CAEP): token lifetime stretches to ~28h but critical events (account disable, password change, refresh-token revocation, risky user) revoke within ~15 min; non-CAE access tokens default 60-90 min. Conditional Access + resilience defaults; PIM for JIT privileged elevation; managed identities vend tokens via IMDS with zero secrets; workload identity federation (OIDC) replaces client secrets. CIAM is a separate 'external tenant' type (Entra External ID), isolated from the workforce tenant. Dogfooding via Secure Future Initiative: phishing-resistant MFA enforced for 99.6% of employees, phishing-resistant credentials enforced in production environments, video-based identity verification for 95% of internal users, PAWs/locked-down AVD for high-risk engineering access. Break-glass: 2+ cloud-only emergency access accounts with FIDO2/cert credentials excluded from Conditional Access.

Converged model: standalone IDCS was retired and merged into OCI IAM 'identity domains' — one engine serving both workforce and customer identity via domain types (Free/Default, Oracle Apps, Premium, External User). The Default domain is the tenancy bootstrap: created with the tenancy, holds the initial administrative user and root IAM policies, and Oracle guidance is to keep it for OCI administrators only — a clean primordial-domain bootstrap pattern. Each domain is deployed redundantly across ADs/fault domains in-region; domains can be replicated to additional subscribed regions for read availability, and regions with cross-region DR get active-passive replication behind a single transparent URL. API surface is natively SCIM 2.0-compliant (the identity domains REST API uses SCIM core schemas + Oracle extensions for users/groups/apps) plus OAuth2/OIDC/SAML2 and FIDO2/passkeys with adaptive security. Service-to-service: instance principals / resource principals — the platform auto-issues and auto-rotates short-lived x509 certificates to compute/resources, which sign API requests (HTTP Signature); authorization via dynamic groups + policy, eliminating distributed API keys.

convergent_patterns: Control plane / data plane split with static stability: authentication+authorization data planes are regionally autonomous, read-replicated, and keep working when the (often single-homed) write/control plane is down — AWS IAM (global control plane, independent per-region data planes), Entra (single write primary per partition, geo-distributed read replicas + Backup Authentication System serving cached evaluations), OCI (home region writes, replica regions), Meta CATs (explicitly no online dependency in the serving path). Writes centralized, reads/validation everywhere.

Credential validation is local/offline in the hot path — no per-request call-home to a central introspection service: SigV4 signature verification against replicated key material (AWS), JWT signature verification (Entra/Cognito/OCI/Identity Platform), symmetric MAC tickets (Meta CATs/STEKs), cert-based ALTS handshakes (Google). All five treat per-request central token introspection as an availability anti-pattern.

Revocation is event/policy-driven, not token-blacklist-driven: short-ish tokens plus an out-of-band revocation channel — Entra CAE/CAEP critical events (~15 min propagation, instant IP-policy enforcement), AWS deny-by-policy on aws:TokenIssueTime, Google central session service + DBSC device binding. Token lifetime and revocation latency are explicitly traded against availability.

Workload/service identity is platform-issued, short-lived, auto-rotated, and bound to the service identity rather than host or network location: Borg Prime-issued ALTS creds, Meta ICA certs minted at container start with identity in an x509 extension, AWS instance-metadata role credentials / Roles Anywhere / EKS Pod Identity, Azure managed identities via IMDS, OCI instance/resource principals with auto-rotated certs. Long-lived static secrets are being systematically exterminated (workload identity federation on AWS/GCP/Azure).

All internal east-west traffic is mutually authenticated and encrypted with workload identity (ALTS, Meta Fizz mTLS, Azure/AWS signed tokens or mTLS) — network location confers zero trust (BeyondCorp; Google infra whitepaper; Meta service encryption).

Phishing-resistant credentials are mandatory for the workforce and the operators of the IdP itself: Google security keys since ~2017 (zero successful phishing, 85k+ employees), Microsoft SFI (99.6% of employees on phishing-resistant MFA, enforced in production environments, PAWs), AWS mandatory root MFA + passkeys; all five ship FIDO2/WebAuthn passkeys in product (Google 400M+ accounts/1B+ sign-ins; Cognito Managed Login passkeys; Entra; OCI identity domains).

Workforce and customer identity are separate planes: AWS Identity Center vs Cognito; Entra workforce tenant vs External ID external tenant; Google Cloud Identity vs Identity Platform; even Oracle's converged service isolates via domain types and keeps the Default (admin) domain free of application users. Customer identities never live in the operator directory.

Standards posture is uniform: OIDC/OAuth2 primary, SAML2 supported for enterprise federation inbound, SCIM 2.0 for provisioning (Oracle goes furthest: SCIM is the native REST API shape). OAuth token exchange (RFC 8693-style) for cross-service identity propagation (AWS trusted identity propagation, Azure WIF, Google federation).

Break-glass access independent of the federation/IdP chain is a hard requirement: Azure emergency-access accounts excluded from Conditional Access with FIDO2/cert creds; AWS break-glass IAM users + centrally managed root; OCI Default domain primordial admin. Everyone assumes the IdP or the external IdP will fail and pre-provisions a path around it.

Multi-region IdP survivability is headline engineering, retrofitted where missing: Entra Backup Authentication System + multi-region replicas; AWS added IAM Identity Center region replication and Cognito multi-Region replication (June 2026); OCI cross-region DR behind one URL; Google identity globally distributed. Default token/auth flows are designed to succeed during regional loss (99.99% Entra SLA, 99.95% design goals at AWS/Google CIAM).
divergences: Proof-of-possession vs bearer: AWS uniquely refuses bearer tokens for its core API plane — every request is SigV4-signed with the secret never on the wire — while Azure/Google/OCI public clouds run on bearer JWTs, and Meta runs symmetric MAC tokens (CATs) because asymmetric crypto was too expensive at billions of RPS. Reason: AWS optimizes for verifiable-offline + replay resistance; Meta for CPU cost + disaster availability; the JWT camp for ecosystem interop.

Custom transport vs standard TLS: Google built ALTS (2007) because TLS of that era was inadequate and identity needed to be service-bound; Meta, building later, chose standard TLS 1.3 (own Fizz implementation) and put custom identity in an x509 extension. Nobody starting today would build an ALTS — the divergence is purely chronological.

Converged vs split workforce/CIAM product: Oracle merged both planes into one service (identity domains with domain types); Microsoft/AWS/Google keep separate products/tenant types. Oracle gains one engine and one ops surface; the others gain hard isolation and independently evolving feature sets.

Global vs regional IdP topology: Entra and Google run globally distributed identity stores; AWS deliberately regionalizes (regional STS endpoints, regional Cognito, region-pinned Identity Center) accepting weaker UX for blast-radius isolation; OCI uses home-region + replicas. AWS's stance: regional pinning is a feature (fault isolation), the others treat global availability as the feature.

Revocation philosophy: Microsoft invests in near-real-time revocation as a product (CAE/CAEP, 28h tokens revoked in ~15 min); AWS explicitly rejects online revocation (policy-condition deny only); Google attacks the problem sideways via credential binding (DBSC, device-bound sessions). Reflects different bets on where revocation cost should live (issuer, policy engine, or client device).

SPIFFE: none of the five uses SPIFFE/SPIRE internally — ALTS/LOAS, Meta ICA, SigV4, dSTS, and instance principals all predate or bypass it; they expose OIDC workload federation at the cloud boundary instead. SPIFFE is the open-source descendant of these systems, not the hyperscaler practice itself.
anti_patterns: Long-lived static secrets for workloads (API keys, client secrets, stored root credentials): AWS now programmatically deletes root credentials from member accounts (Nov 2024); Azure managed identities and workload identity federation exist explicitly to eliminate secrets; OCI instance principals replace distributed keys.
Network-location trust / VPN perimeter: retired by BeyondCorp (2014+); Google and Meta authenticate+encrypt all internal RPC regardless of network; 'internal network' confers no privilege.

Per-request online token introspection against a central store: Meta CATs were designed specifically to avoid online auth dependencies in disasters; AWS's irrevocable temp creds and Entra's cached backup auth make the same call — a synchronous IdP dependency in every request path is a global SPOF.
Standalone/siloed CIAM products: Oracle retired standalone IDCS into IAM identity domains; Microsoft superseded Azure AD B2C with Entra External ID external tenants for new CIAM deployments.
Mixing customer/application users into the workforce or admin directory: Entra External ID isolates external tenants; Oracle explicitly warns the Default domain is for OCI administrators only.

SMS/OTP MFA for workforce and privileged users: Google replaced with mandatory security keys (zero phishing since); Microsoft SFI mandates phishing-resistant MFA and is removing weaker methods; passkeys now outpace SMS+app OTP combined at Google.
IdP without pre-provisioned break-glass outside the federation chain (tenant lockout): all vendors mandate emergency-access accounts/break-glass IAM users excluded from normal policy.

Region-pinned single-instance workforce SSO with no replica: AWS IAM Identity Center's primary-region-only design had to be retrofitted with region replication, and Cognito only gained multi-Region replication in June 2026 — both are cautionary tales about bolting on IdP DR later.

Building bespoke transport security protocols today: Google's own framing is that ALTS exists because 2007-era TLS was inadequate; Meta's choice of standard TLS 1.3 + custom cert extension is the modern pattern.

Trusting the primary IdP implementation as a single point of failure: Microsoft built an entirely separate Backup Authentication System with independent code/cache rather than only hardening the primary.
oyatie_prescriptions: Split the IdP into a write control plane and a cell-replicated authentication data plane from day one (AWS IAM / Entra Core Store pattern): single-homed writes per partition with synchronous durable replication to a second cell before ack; every cell serves authn + Cedar authorization from local replicated state and stays statically stable when the control plane is down. Align IdP partitions with ADR-0341/0348 cells and shuffle-shard tenants across IdP cells so one tenant's load or poison-pill cannot take out the identity plane.

Make every credential verifiable offline in the request hot path: short-lived signed access tokens (JWT/JOSE; consider COSE/CWT for internal compactness) validated against cell-locally replicated JWKS — never a synchronous introspection call to a central token store. Budget: token verify + Cedar evaluate must be in-process per request, Cedar policy/entity data replicated to cells like the AWS IAM data plane replicates policy.

Implement revocation as events + policy, not blacklists: (a) OpenID Shared Signals/CAEP-style revocation event channel to resource services with a ~15-minute propagation SLO (Entra CAE), letting you stretch token lifetimes for resilience; (b) AWS-style policy revocation — a Cedar condition denying tokens with issue_time earlier than a per-principal cutoff, effective on next evaluation with zero distributed state; (c) plan Device Bound Session Credentials (DBSC)-style key-bound web sessions to neutralize cookie/token theft.

Service-to-service identity: platform-issued, auto-rotated short-lived x509 workload certs minted at pod start by your own internal CA, with the service identity (not hostname) in the cert — Meta ICA / OCI instance-principal pattern. Use standard TLS 1.3 via rustls (do NOT build an ALTS); adopt SPIFFE-compatible identity naming (spiffe://cell/ns/service) since you are on k8s and it is the open-standard descendant of ALTS/LOAS — then authorize callers in Cedar by workload identity. For high-QPS internal paths where asymmetric resumption costs bite, use Meta-style session tickets with per-identity derived STEKs and a previous/current/next key rotation window.

Eliminate long-lived secrets structurally: workloads get identity from the platform (cert or token via a metadata/agent endpoint, the IMDS/instance-principal pattern); external systems (CI, partner clouds) get in via OIDC workload identity federation / RFC 8693 token exchange — no static API keys anywhere in the substrate. This also gives you trusted identity propagation (end-user context flows through token exchange, the Google EUC-ticket / AWS TIP pattern) so downstream services authorize on the real end user, not just the calling service.

Separate workforce and customer identity planes inside one converged engine (Oracle identity-domains / Entra External ID hybrid — right fit for a Rust monorepo): one Rust IdP codebase, hard-partitioned 'domains' with isolated user stores, key material, and branding; a primordial Default/operator domain created at substrate bootstrap holding only operator identities and root policies — application/customer users are forbidden there. This maps cleanly onto single-tenant→multi-tenant: each customer tenant is a domain (or shares a pooled domain partition), shuffle-sharded across cells.

Bootstrap + dogfood story: the IdP authenticates its own operators via its workforce domain with mandatory hardware-backed passkeys/security keys (Google: zero successful phishing across 85k+ employees since enforcement); operator/production access goes through PIM-style JIT elevation with approval and expiry, from hardened workstations (Microsoft SFI PAW pattern). Provision >=2 break-glass credentials that bypass federation and conditional policy — FIDO2-based, sealed offline, alarmed on use, tested quarterly (Azure emergency-access pattern) — plus an AWS-style centrally managed 'root' for tenant cells so no long-lived root credentials exist per cell.

Passkeys/WebAuthn are v1 table stakes, not a fast-follow: passwordless-default for workforce; passkeys + email OTP for customers with SMS only as a legacy escape hatch. All five hyperscalers shipped this; Google's 400M-account/1B-sign-in numbers prove consumer viability.

Standards surface: OIDC + OAuth2 (incl. token exchange RFC 8693, PKCE, DPoP for sender-constraining where feasible) as primary; SAML2 inbound-only for enterprise customer federation; SCIM 2.0 both as the provisioning protocol AND (Oracle pattern) as the native shape of your user/group REST API — dogfooding SCIM as your own API eliminates a translation layer and is a differentiator audit-ready enterprises expect.

Multi-region/multi-cell survivability with explicit SLOs (per ADR-0130 OpenSLO authoring): target >=99.99% authentication availability; active read replicas in >=2 regions behind one stable issuer URL (OCI transparent-URL DR pattern); and a minimal independent backup-auth path — cached last-known-good claims + Entra-style 'resilience defaults' policy evaluation — so a bug in the primary IdP code path cannot take down all authentication. Do NOT region-pin the workforce SSO instance; AWS Identity Center's retrofit shows the cost.

Token lifetime policy: customer/workforce access tokens default ~1h (configurable 5min-24h), rotating refresh tokens 30-90d, workload certs/tokens minutes-to-hours auto-rotated; longer-lived (24h+) sessions permitted only for CAE-capable clients subscribed to the revocation channel. Per-use-case key separation with routine automated rotation through your async job substrate (Meta ACS pattern).

research.domain: Authorization at scale (RBAC + ABAC + PBAC unified): PDP/PEP topology, policy engines, consistency, caching, policy-as-code CI, audit, multi-tenant isolation

per_company.approach: Three proven layers. (1) IAM data plane: default-deny, explicit-deny-overrides evaluation; handles >500M authorization API calls/sec worldwide; deliberately EVENTUALLY CONSISTENT (policy changes take seconds+ to propagate) to keep the data plane highly available and low-latency; evaluation happens regionally inside the request path, not via a remote PDP hop. (2) Automated reasoning as production infrastructure: Zelkova (FMCAD'18) translates IAM policies to SMT (strings+regex+bitvectors) and answers properties over ALL possible requests, powering IAM Access Analyzer and S3 Block Public Access; ~1 billion SMT queries/day via cvc5. (3) Cedar + Amazon Verified Permissions (OOPSLA'24 paper): one language unifying RBAC (principal-group policies), ABAC (when/unless attribute conditions), ReBAC (entity hierarchy + template-linked per-resource policies); deny-by-default, forbid-overrides-permit; deliberately NOT Turing-complete (no recursion/loops) so evaluation always terminates and SMT analysis is decidable/sound/complete; formalized in Lean with verified slicing and validation; Rust implementation; policy slicing gives 4.0us (Drive-like) and 11us p99 (GitHub-like) — 28.7–35.2x faster than OpenFGA, 42.8–80.8x faster than Rego. AVP = Cedar PDP-as-a-service: policy stores with schemas, BatchIsAuthorized (up to 30 decisions/call; demonstrated 800ms→79ms list filtering), default 200 TPS quota (raised from 30 in Mar 2024), decision caching at API Gateway authorizer (120s default TTL), CloudTrail data events log isAuthorized decisions (opt-in, decision in additionalEventData). AWS explicitly documents BOTH topologies: central managed PDP (AVP) with PEPs at gateway/microservices, OR Cedar SDK embedded as in-process library when latency/connectivity demands it. Multi-tenant guidance: policy-store-per-tenant (isolation, independent schema, compliance) vs shared store with tenant attributes (cheaper, noisy-neighbor risk); hybrid recommended.

Two distinct systems, deliberately. (1) Zanzibar (USENIX ATC'19) for product/user-facing sharing: pure relationship-based (ReBAC) tuples (object#relation@user) in Spanner, one DB per namespace; userset-rewrite rules (computed_userset, tuple_to_userset, union/intersection/exclusion); serves Drive/YouTube/Photos/Calendar. Scale: 2+ trillion tuples (~100TB), >10M QPS aggregate (4.2M Check, 8.2M Read, 760K Expand, 25K Write), >10,000 servers, dozens of clusters, p95 <10ms for Safe requests, 99.999% availability over 3 years. Consistency: zookies (opaque timestamp tokens) solve the 'new enemy' problem — client stores zookie with content version, checks are at-least-as-fresh; ~99% of checks served from local replicas at moderate staleness (median 3ms, p95 9ms). Hot-spot machinery: consistent-hash distributed cache, lock tables deduping in-flight checks, Leopard denormalized index for deep/wide group nesting, request hedging for tail latency. (2) Cloud IAM for infrastructure: role bindings (RBAC) + IAM Conditions in CEL (ABAC, incl. resource tags, time, request attrs) + deny policies (evaluated FIRST) + principal access boundary policies; eventually consistent — changes typically effective in ~2 min, can take 7+ min; Cloud Audit Logs record decisions per auditConfig. Folder/project hierarchy is the structural scope.

Internal platform, three public artifacts. (1) Graph-native viewer-context authorization: privacy rules attached to entities in the Ent framework over TAO — every read/write carries a viewer context and evaluates an Allow/Deny rule chain at data-fetch time (the open-source entgo.io privacy layer is the public descendant); authorization lives in the data-access framework, not per-endpoint code. (2) IVD (IEEE S&P 2017): defense-in-depth invariant learner — infers >200,000 likely authorization invariants daily from ~500M sampled requests and checks them every second against millions of writes to a graph of trillions of entities; caught and blocked real authz bypasses before code fixes shipped — an explicit admission that handwritten checks get missed at scale. (3) Privacy Aware Infrastructure / Policy Zones (2024–25 engineering blogs): information-flow control for purpose limitation — data assets (millions) annotated with labels; labels propagate at runtime through HHVM, Presto, Spark function calls and SQL; rollout pattern is logging-mode-then-enforcement-mode; 10x compute-efficiency gains via lattice simplification; explicitly COMPLEMENTS ACLs: ACLs answer 'who can access', Policy Zones answers 'for what purpose may data flow'. Meta's position: access control alone is insufficient for privacy guarantees at scale.

RBAC-first with bolted-on ABAC and best-in-class JIT elevation. Azure Resource Manager evaluates: deny assignments FIRST (deny assignments are deliberately not user-creatable in general — only via Blueprints/managed apps), then role assignments narrowed by scope (management group → subscription → resource group → resource). Hard limit: 4,000 role assignments per subscription (fixed, non-negotiable — forces group-based assignment hygiene). ABAC = conditions attached to role assignments; GA only for Storage (Blobs, ADLS Gen2, Queues) using @Request/@Resource/@Environment/@Principal attributes (principal attrs from Entra custom security attributes); condition changes take up to 5 min to enforce; documented caveat that list operations don't filter per-blob — listing can show names the caller can't read. Entra PIM is the industry-reference JIT model: 'eligible' vs 'active' assignments; activation gated on MFA, business justification, approval workflow; time-bound with auto-revocation; eligible assignments don't count against the 4,000 limit; PIM composes with ABAC conditions (though principal attributes unsupported in PIM conditions). Azure Policy (resource governance PBAC) is kept as a separate engine from request-time RBAC.

The minimalist outlier, and deliberately so. Compartments (nested containers, policy inheritance down the tree) are the primary authorization scope — the structural isolation primitive. Policy language is human-readable sentences: 'Allow group X to <verb> <resource-type> in compartment Y where <conditions>'. Exactly four verbs forming a strict permission lattice: inspect < read < use < manage — a fixed coarse-grained vocabulary instead of per-API action strings. ALLOW-ONLY: no deny statements exist at all; implicit default deny is the only deny. ABAC via where-clause condition variables (request.principal.id, request.networkSource, tag-based policies on principals and resources — 'Deep Dive into Tag based OCI IAM Policies'). Policy attachment location (tenancy vs compartment) controls who may modify the policy — delegation of policy administration follows the resource hierarchy. Best practice guidance warns against any-user grants. The bet: a small, analyzable, monotonic (allow-only) language plus strong structural compartments beats an expressive language with deny-conflict resolution.

convergent_patterns: Default-deny everywhere, with deny-as-override where deny exists at all: AWS IAM (explicit deny wins), Cedar (forbid overrides permit), Azure (deny assignments evaluated first), Google Cloud IAM (deny policies evaluated first), OCI (implicit deny only). No hyperscaler uses ordered/first-match policy semantics — all are order-independent set evaluation.

No single model survives: every hyperscaler converged on roles for manageability + attribute conditions for granularity + relationships for user-facing sharing. AWS IAM conditions, Cedar RBAC+ABAC+ReBAC in one language, Azure RBAC+ABAC conditions, Google roles+CEL conditions+Zanzibar tuples, OCI groups+where clauses. RBAC/ABAC/PBAC unification in one engine is the destination, verified shipped in Cedar (OOPSLA'24).

Coarse structural container checked before fine-grained policy: AWS accounts/OUs+SCPs, Azure management groups/subscriptions, Google folders/projects, OCI compartments, Meta product zones. The cheap hierarchical scope check is the first isolation gate and the tenant boundary; fine-grained evaluation happens inside it.

Authorization data plane is local + eventually consistent; freshness is an explicit contract only where it matters: AWS IAM (seconds), Google Cloud IAM (2–7 min), Azure conditions (5 min) all accept staleness for availability; Zanzibar is the only one exposing client-controlled bounded staleness (zookies) — because content-sharing revocation demands it. Convergent lesson: pick staleness per use-case and make it visible, never accidental.

Evaluation happens at microsecond-to-single-digit-ms latency near the request, with policy distribution centralized: Zanzibar serves 99% of 10M+ QPS from local replicas (3ms median, <10ms p95); AWS evaluates IAM in-region inline; Cedar embedded evaluates in 4–11us via verified policy slicing; AVP-remote-PDP is the exception and AWS itself documents embedding the Cedar SDK when latency matters. Central policy store + distributed evaluation is the converged topology.

Policy-as-code with automated reasoning in CI is proven hyperscaler practice, not research: Zelkova/Access Analyzer run ~1B SMT queries/day in production; Cedar ships a verified (Lean) SMT symbolic compiler for policy equivalence/invariant checking; Google ships custom org-policy constraints in CEL; Meta's IVD machine-learns 200k invariants/day as a safety net. All five treat 'does any policy permit X' as a decidable, mechanically-checked question.

Decision audit logs (allow AND deny) as first-class, opt-in at data-event volume: AVP isAuthorized decisions to CloudTrail data events, Google Cloud Audit Logs per auditConfig, Azure Activity Log, Meta's logging-mode-before-enforcement-mode rollout discipline for new policies.

Deliberately constrained policy languages: Cedar excludes recursion/loops to guarantee termination and decidable analysis; OCI restricts to 4 verbs and allow-only; Azure restricts who can create denies; Zanzibar restricts to set-algebra rewrites. Expressiveness is traded away for analyzability and bounded latency — none of the five adopted a Turing-complete language (contrast OPA/Rego) for their core authz path.

Time-bound and JIT permissions converging as standard: Entra PIM eligible/active with MFA+approval+auto-expiry; Google IAM condition-based expirations; AWS short-lived STS credentials and session policies. Standing privilege is treated as the defect.
divergences: Deny semantics: OCI has NO deny statements (monotonic allow-only language, betting on analyzability); AWS/Google/Azure/Cedar all have deny-overrides. Azure splits the difference — denies exist but ordinary users cannot author them. The disagreement is about whether deny is a guardrail primitive or a footgun.

Data model: graph/tuple ReBAC (Zanzibar, Meta TAO/Ent) vs attribute-evaluation policy languages (AWS IAM, Cedar, Azure, OCI, Google Cloud IAM). Google runs BOTH and keeps them separate: Zanzibar for consumer sharing (billions of users, trillions of tuples), CEL-conditioned RBAC for cloud infrastructure. Cedar claims the unification (parent-entity ReBAC + templates) but at hyperscale Google chose specialization.

PDP topology: AWS sells both central-remote (AVP, ~200 TPS default quota, 120s PEP cache) and embedded-library (Cedar SDK, microseconds); Zanzibar is a dedicated central fleet (10k+ servers) made viable only by heavy caching/hedging; Azure/OCI evaluate inside the platform control plane (invisible to customers). There is no consensus that a remote PDP is acceptable on hot paths — quota numbers (200 TPS) vs Zanzibar (10M QPS) show remote PDP-as-product is orders of magnitude behind embedded/dedicated designs.

Consistency contract: Zanzibar gives clients zookies (causally-consistent, bounded-stale checks); AWS/Azure/Google Cloud IAM just document 'eventually consistent, wait seconds-to-minutes' with no client-visible token. Divergence driven by use-case: document-sharing revocation needs causal ordering; infrastructure role changes tolerate minutes.

ABAC coverage: AWS condition keys are universal across services; Google CEL conditions broad but with a limited attribute catalog; Azure ABAC is GA only for Storage services — Microsoft chose deep per-service integration over breadth. OCI conditions exist but the language stays intentionally coarse.

Meta diverges philosophically: invests in information-flow control (Policy Zones) on top of access control, asserting ACLs cannot express purpose limitation; no other hyperscaler enforces purpose at runtime in the data plane. Meta also uniquely deploys ML-learned invariants (IVD) as a runtime authz-bug net.

Multi-tenant policy isolation: AWS guidance genuinely forks — per-tenant policy store (hard isolation, per-tenant schema, compliance) vs shared store with tenant-attribute ABAC (cost, noisy-neighbor risk) with a hybrid recommendation; Zanzibar instead isolates by namespace-per-client with per-namespace Spanner databases. No converged answer; isolation granularity is a real design decision.
anti_patterns: Authorization logic embedded ad hoc in application code — the explicit motivation for Cedar, Zanzibar, and Meta's framework-level Ent privacy rules; Meta built IVD precisely because hand-written per-feature checks get missed at trillions-of-entities scale.

Turing-complete or recursive policy languages on the hot path: Cedar deliberately omits recursion/loops/arbitrary functions to guarantee termination and decidable SMT analysis; benchmark gap vs Rego (42–80x) is presented as the cost of unbounded expressiveness.

Naive TTL decision caching without an invalidation/freshness contract: the Zanzibar 'new enemy problem' is the canonical failure (ACL update reordered against content update); AWS documents that API Gateway authorizer caching delays revocation and doesn't support invalidation for Lambda authorizers — known, accepted, bounded risk, never silent.

Synchronous cross-region reads per check: Zanzibar's entire architecture (local replicas, Safe-vs-Recent request split, Leopard index, hedging) exists to avoid this; 99% of checks never leave the region.

Deny-statement sprawl as a routine management tool: OCI omitted deny entirely; Azure blocks user-created deny assignments; AWS guidance steers structural guardrails to SCPs rather than scattered explicit denies. Retired idea: using denies for everyday revocation instead of removing allows.

Wildcard principal grants: OCI best practices explicitly recommend against any-user; AWS Access Analyzer exists largely to flag unintended public/cross-account access (S3 Block Public Access built on Zelkova).

Treating list-time filtering as authorization: Azure ABAC documents that list operations may reveal blob names the caller cannot read — enumeration and access must be separately authorized (and batch-authz used for list filtering, per AVP).
Per-role direct user assignments at scale: Azure's fixed 4,000 role-assignment cap is a forcing function — group/role indirection is mandatory, per-user grants are the retired pattern.
Standing privileged access: Entra PIM's whole existence retires permanently-active admin roles in favor of eligible+activate-with-approval.

Big-bang enforcement of new policy regimes: Meta runs Policy Zones in logging mode before enforcement mode; AVP/Access Analyzer pattern is analyze-then-enforce. Turning on enforcement without a shadow/observe phase is the anti-pattern.
oyatie_prescriptions: PDP topology: embed the cedar-policy Rust crate as an in-process library PDP inside every axum service — Cedar's own paper shows 4.0–11us p99 with verified policy slicing, vs ~200 TPS default quota for AVP's remote PDP. Never put a network hop in the per-request decision path. Build a central control-plane policy-store service (Rust/axum) that compiles, validates, versions, signs, and pushes policy sets + schemas to cells via the content-addressed delivery fabric (ADR-0516+ buck2 artifacts are a natural fit: policy bundles as content-addressed artifacts).

Align policy-store partitioning with cells (ADR-0341/0348): each cell carries only the policy slices and entity data of its resident tenants (AVP per-tenant-store isolation + Zanzibar namespace-per-client, unified). Tenant = Cedar namespace; shuffle-sharding already bounds noisy-neighbor blast radius — extend that to authz by rate-limiting authorization-relevant entity-write QPS per tenant.

Unify RBAC+ABAC+PBAC in Cedar exactly as AVP customers do: RBAC via principal-group membership (principal in Role::"tenant-admin") resolved at token issuance into JWT claims (one round trip, no group lookup at check time); ABAC via when/unless attribute conditions; per-resource sharing grants via Cedar policy templates instantiated per (principal, resource) — the documented AVP template pattern; ReBAC via entity parent hierarchies (resource in Folder::X).

Deny discipline (learn from OCI + Azure): additive permits are the routine mechanism; forbid policies are reserved for a small set of machine-enforced structural guardrails — above all 'forbid unless resource.tenant == principal.tenant' as the cell-level tenant-isolation invariant. No human-authored ad hoc forbids for everyday revocation; revocation = remove the permit/group edge.

Adopt an explicit freshness-token contract (zookie-equivalent) from day one: every policy bundle and entity snapshot carries a monotonic version; PEPs report the version evaluated; decision caches key on (request-hash, policy-version) so policy pushes invalidate structurally rather than by TTL. Set a published revocation SLO — p99 enforcement of a revocation < 60s across all cells (beats Azure's 5 min and Google's 7 min, and is the kind of trailblazing bar Oyatie wants). Author it as an OpenSLO per the ADR-0130 observability mandate.

Latency budgets, Zanzibar-calibrated: in-process Cedar check < 100us p99 (paper shows 11us is achievable); end-to-end authz overhead per request < 1ms p99 including entity fetch; any future remote check service (e.g., for cross-service relationship checks) gets the Zanzibar bar: p95 < 10ms, 99.999% availability, served from cell-local replicas.

Entity/relationship data: store relationship tuples Zanzibar-style ((object, relation, subject) rows, cell-local) and hydrate Cedar entities from them at the PEP; precompute deep/wide group closures asynchronously (Leopard-index analog) rather than recursive expansion at check time; dedupe concurrent identical checks (lock-table pattern) in the axum middleware layer.

Policy CI in the buck2 monorepo (Zelkova-grade, not lint-grade): every policy change goes through (1) cedar schema validation, (2) differential golden-request test suites per tenant archetype, (3) Cedar symbolic/SMT analysis asserting standing invariants — 'no policy permits cross-tenant access', 'no permit on admin actions without MFA attribute', 'new policy set is not more permissive than predecessor unless flagged' — wired into oya-ci (ADR-0513) as a merge-blocking gate. AWS runs a billion SMT checks/day; Oyatie running thousands is trivially affordable.

Ship BatchIsAuthorized semantics in the first authz API: list-endpoint filtering via a single batched call over 30+ (resource, action) pairs — AVP measured 800ms→79ms; this prevents the N+1 authz-call anti-pattern from ever entering the codebase.

Decision audit as a first-class event stream: every allow AND deny emits a structured event (decision, determining policy IDs, policy-bundle version, principal, action, resource, tenant, latency) into cloud/observability; deny events always at 100%, allow events sampled with per-tenant override to 100% for compliance tenants. This is the AVP-CloudTrail-data-events pattern, dogfooded on the owned observability substrate.

JIT elevation (PIM-equivalent) rather than standing admin: model eligible vs active role membership as entities with expiry attributes; an elevation workflow service (approval + step-up auth + justification) writes short-lived membership edges; Cedar conditions check activation expiry. Eligible memberships excluded from any assignment-count guardrails, mirroring Azure.

Rollout discipline: every new policy class ships in logging/shadow mode first (Meta Policy Zones pattern) — evaluate-and-log divergence between old and new policy bundles before enforcement flips, gated by the ADR-0130 SLO promotion pipeline. Later roadmap (separate system, not conflated with Cedar): an IVD-style invariant learner over write traffic as defense-in-depth, and purpose-limitation data labels as an IFC layer above access control.
