research.domain: Multi-tenant SaaS + cell-based architecture (tenant isolation models, cell sizing/placement/migration, thin global layer, noisy-neighbor controls, control-plane/data-plane doctrine, degraded-mode/static stability)

per_company.approach: Most codified doctrine of the five. (1) SaaS Lens defines silo/pool/bridge tenant isolation: silo = dedicated stack per tenant (regulated/premium, kills noisy neighbor, costs idle capacity), pool = shared infra, bridge = per-microservice mix; tenant TIER is the input that decides the model, and cost-per-tenant attribution (metering tenant consumption, correlating to bill — SaaS Lens COST_1/COST_2) is a first-class requirement because basic-tier tenants typically dominate infra cost while generating least revenue. (2) 'Reducing the Scope of Impact with Cell-Based Architecture' whitepaper: a cell is a complete, state-isolated replica of the workload keyed by a partition key aligned to the service 'grain'; components = cell router ('thinnest possible layer' — routing and ONLY routing), cells, and a control plane that provisions/migrates/monitors cells. Cell sizing: cap max cell size, keep sizes consistent, three opposing forces (big enough for largest workload + economies of scale, small enough to TEST AT FULL SCALE and stay below quota/scaling cliffs); every cell must have a known limit (TPS, tenants, GB). Cell placement is a control-plane competency requiring per-cell capacity observability and headroom below tested max for failover (REL01-BP06). Cell migration is expected for stateful systems: clone → flip authoritative → redirect → forget, with cross-cell redirects/dual mapping during transition; oversized tenants get a dedicated cell. (3) Control/data plane doctrine (MacCárthaigh/Brooker): data plane is O(N) on the request path and AP-leaning; control plane scales differently, is 'statistically more likely to fail', is CP-leaning; recovery must NOT depend on the control plane (REL11-BP04 static stability) — e.g., the cell router loads tenant→cell routes into memory from S3 and keeps routing through control-plane outage. (4) Shuffle sharding (Route 53): 2048 virtual name servers, each domain on a shard of 4 → ~730 billion possible shards, no two customer domains share more than 2 name servers — pooled fleet, near-single-tenant blast radius; same pattern in Hyperplane. (5) Physalia (NSDI '20): EBS config master built as 'millions of tiny databases' — one ~7-node Paxos cell per volume, topology-aware placement to minimize blast radius and partition probability; proves cell-per-resource at extreme granularity in production. (6) Noisy neighbor: Builders' Library 'Fairness in multi-tenant systems' — per-tenant token buckets at admission, composed buckets (low-rate/high-burst + high-rate/low-burst) to bound bursts, quotas raised as tenants grow organically, heavy-hitters/top-talkers/counting-Bloom-filter algorithms for high-cardinality fairness.

Internal: Borg (EuroSys '15) manages compute in 'cells' — median cell ~10,000 machines, one Borgmaster (5x replicated) per cell; the cell is simultaneously the scheduling, management, and failure domain; Google runs many cells rather than one giant fleet. Data layer: Spanner moves data in 'directories' between Paxos groups automatically (live rebalancing is the platform's job, not the app's); Cloud Spanner multi-tenancy docs enumerate the full tenancy spectrum — instance-, database-, schema-, and table-level (row-keyed by tenant) — with explicit guidance to mix per tier; multi-region Spanner = 5 replicas across 3+ regions with a witness region, dual-region configs for data residency. Resource model is rigorously zonal/regional/global, and Google is the most explicit about the danger of the global tier: SRE book's 'Global Chubby Planned Outage' — global Chubby was so reliable that teams silently took hard dependencies on it, so SRE deliberately takes it down each quarter it overshoots its SLO to flush out unreasonable global dependencies. Doctrine: global services are allowed but must be distrusted by construction; serve from regional replicas, degrade gracefully when the global layer is gone.

No public cloud; the region is the cell and placement is solver-driven and continuous. (1) Shard Manager (SOSP '21): generic shard-placement control plane managing ~100M shards for hundreds of applications on >1M servers serving billions of RPS; placement expressed in a constraint DSL fed to a constraint solver (Meta explicitly migrated OFF hand-tuned heuristics); spreads replicas across fault domains/regions; handles millions of maintenance events/month; graceful shard migration forwards in-flight requests and drains before container restarts (70% of apps use graceful drain); control-plane state in ZooKeeper, routing state pushed to clients via service discovery — clients keep routing when the control plane is down. (2) TAO (ATC '13): social-graph store sharded with a master region per shard; each region has follower + leader cache tiers over regional MySQL; writes forward to the master region, async replication (<1s lag), eventual consistency — read-optimized regional cells over a thin cross-region write path, ~billion reads/sec. (3) Taiji (SOSP '19): edge→datacenter user-traffic assignment as a constraint-optimization problem; connection-aware routing ('social hashing' of connected users to the same datacenter) cut backend load 17%; in production 4+ years. (4) RAS (SOSP '21) + Global Reservations/Regional Fluidity: region-wide continuous capacity re-optimization accounting for hierarchical fault domains, correlated failures, and maintenance — capacity buffers for region loss are precomputed. (5) Defcon (OSDI '23): graceful feature degradation as a platform — product features annotated with criticality-level 'knobs', knobs auto-tested for product/infra trade-offs, used in real incidents across Facebook/Messenger/Instagram/WhatsApp to shed load by turning off features, not dropping users.

(1) Deployment Stamps pattern (Azure Architecture Center): stamp = scale unit/cell = independent copy of ALL components including data stores, serving a predefined tenant subset; scale ~linearly by adding stamps; minimum TWO stamps always (a single stamp breeds hard-coded assumptions); stamps double as deployment rings (risk-averse tenants on slow-update stamps); capacity per stamp defined by a proxy metric (tenant count) with proactive stamp provisioning; tenant→stamp routing via a directory — reference design: Front Door (global anycast) → regional API Management gateways doing tenant→stamp lookup in a geo-replicated Cosmos DB mapping store (the routing layer is itself a geode); the docs explicitly warn that moving tenants between stamps is hard, requires custom backplane logic, and that cross-stamp reporting needs a separate aggregation pipeline; governance drift across many stamps is countered with Azure Policy-as-code. (2) Multitenant guidance mirrors silo/pool/bridge ('tenancy models') and pushes tiering: large customers on single-tenant stamps, small customers pooled. (3) Platform practice: Safe Deployment Practices — all Azure changes flow through canary → pilot → progressively broader production rings with automated health gating (Gandalf AIOps), full rollout takes >1 week; Availability Zones as physically isolated intra-region bulkheads. (4) Heritage: Service Fabric (stateful placement/failover platform behind Cosmos DB, SQL DB, Event Hubs) is the internal ancestor of the stamp discipline; mission-critical reference architecture formalizes ephemeral 'scale units' that are replaced, not mutated.

Pushes isolation UP the stack further than anyone: the realm. A realm is a set of regions with its OWN control plane and data plane, sharing no infrastructure, accounts, identity, or network with other realms; customer data cannot leave the realm; commercial (OC1), multiple US/UK government realms, air-gapped National Security Regions, EU Sovereign Cloud realm, and each Dedicated Region customer gets its own realm — i.e., the entire cloud as a silo-able unit (strongest single-tenant story among the five, directly relevant to single-tenant enterprise sales). Within a region: availability domains (isolated DCs, independent power/cooling/network) each containing exactly 3 fault domains (anti-affinity hardware groups with redundant power) — placement against FDs is a first-class API parameter. Two-region-per-country strategy for in-country DR. Public engineering detail on internal service cellularization is thin compared to AWS/Meta (mostly podcasts/'First Principles' blogs, e.g., Pradeep Vincent's 'at scale, anything that can fail will'); treat OCI's contribution as the realm/Dedicated Region isolation model and the rigid region/AD/FD hierarchy, not as a published cell doctrine.

convergent_patterns: Cell/stamp/shard as a capped, fully self-contained bulkhead: every company converges on 'complete copy of the workload, sharing NO state with siblings, with a tested maximum size' — AWS caps cell size so a full-size cell can be load-tested and stays below quota cliffs; Azure stamps have a defined tenant capacity and a two-stamp minimum; Borg cells cap at ~10k machines; Meta shards are the unit of placement; OCI fixes 3 FDs per AD. Scale out = add cells; never grow a cell past its tested limit.

Thin, statically-stable global layer: the only things allowed to be global are routing/tenant-directory, identity, and aggregation — and the routing tier must keep working from cached/last-known-good state when the control plane dies. AWS: cell router is 'the thinnest possible layer' serving routes cached from S3; Azure: geo-replicated tenant→stamp directory behind Front Door, routing layer built as a geode; Meta: routing state pushed into clients via service discovery, control plane in ZooKeeper can fail without stopping traffic; Google: global services exist but get deliberate synthetic outages (Chubby) to keep dependencies honest.

Control plane / data plane separation with asymmetric guarantees: data plane is on the request path, scales O(N), prefers availability over freshness (AP, serves stale config); control plane provisions/places/migrates, scales with change rate, prefers consistency and is EXPECTED to fail more often (CP). Recovery and steady-state must not require the control plane (AWS REL11-BP04; Brooker; Meta Shard Manager; Azure SDP treats deployment as the control-plane risk). 3+ companies state this almost verbatim.

Tenant→cell placement and LIVE migration are control-plane core competencies, not afterthoughts: AWS prescribes clone→flip→redirect→forget with dual-mapping during transition and dedicated cells for whale tenants; Meta runs continuous solver-driven rebalancing with graceful request forwarding/drain; Azure explicitly warns stamps without a migration backplane trap tenants; Google Spanner moves directories automatically. Placement inputs converge on: per-cell capacity + used headroom, tenant size over time, cost-of-move, affinity/anti-affinity.

Tiered isolation (bridge model) everywhere: premium/regulated tenants → silo (dedicated cell/stamp/realm), long tail → pooled cells with logical isolation; tenant tier drives placement, throttles, update cadence, and pricing. AWS SaaS Lens, Azure stamps (single-tenant stamps beside multitenant ones), OCI Dedicated Region/realms, Google Spanner instance→table tenancy spectrum all encode this.

Noisy-neighbor control = admission-time token buckets per tenant, composed/hierarchical, with tier-based quotas that grow with organic usage; fairness telemetry (heavy hitters/top talkers) for high-cardinality cases; throttle BEFORE doing expensive work (AWS fairness article; Azure APIM gateway offloading/throttling at the routing tier; Google per-project quotas; Meta degrades features rather than tenants under overload).

Combinatorial/solver-based assignment to decorrelate tenant failure: AWS shuffle sharding (k-of-n worker subsets per tenant, bounded pairwise overlap → blast radius ~ 1/C(n,k)); Meta and Google reach the same decorrelation via constraint solvers spreading shards/tasks across fault domains; Physalia adds topology-aware placement. The shared principle: tenant→infrastructure assignment is a designed mathematical object, not incidental.

Deployment is treated as the #1 cause of correlated failure, so rollout order is cell-by-cell/ring-by-ring with bake time and automated health gates: Azure SDP (canary → rings, >1 week, Gandalf gating), AWS cell deployment waves + one-box, Google canarying/SRE error budgets, Meta knob-tested gradual pushes. Cells exist largely so deployments have somewhere small to fail.

Degraded-mode operation is designed-in, not improvised: static stability (keep serving with stale data through dependency loss — AWS), feature-level shedding with pre-tested criticality knobs (Meta Defcon), planned outages of global dependencies (Google), self-preservation pillar (Azure RE:07).
divergences: Where the cell boundary sits: AWS draws cells WITHIN a region (AZ- or region-scoped, many cells per service per region); Meta's effective cell IS the region (TAO master regions, RAS region-wide allocation, Taiji routes users between regions); Azure stamps usually equal 'tenant group in a region'; OCI escalates to whole-cloud realms; Google layers both (Borg cell ≈ cluster inside a campus, plus regional Spanner). Driver: AWS sells regional independence; Meta runs one global product; OCI sells sovereignty.

Smart vs dumb vs client-side routing: AWS doctrine wants the dumbest possible router (DNS/Route 53 with 100% data-plane SLA, or an in-memory route table refreshed from S3); Azure's reference design is a smart gateway (APIM doing per-request directory lookups in Cosmos DB); Meta pushes routing into fat clients via service discovery. Trade: dumb router = static stability and simplicity; smart gateway = central policy/offloading; client routing = no middle hop but heavy client SDK investment.

Static combinatorial assignment vs continuous optimization: AWS shuffle sharding is deliberately static and simple (assignments rarely move; statically stable, auditable math); Meta (Shard Manager, Taiji, RAS) and Google (Borg scheduler, Spanner directory movement) continuously re-solve placement for utilization and locality. Trade: utilization and locality vs moving-parts risk; Meta accepts a powerful always-on control plane that AWS doctrine would distrust.

Data partitioning default: AWS SaaS guidance is comfortable with pooled row-level tenancy scoped by per-tenant IAM policy and DB-per-cell silos; Azure heritage favors database-per-tenant (elastic pools) with stamps around them; Google pushes shared-schema on Spanner because the database itself reshards live (the platform absorbs the rebalancing problem apps otherwise solve with cells). Your DB primitive determines how much cell machinery you need.

Migration posture: Meta treats tenant/shard movement as a continuous background process (millions of maintenance events/month absorbed automatically); AWS and Azure treat tenant-to-cell moves as exceptional, explicitly-costed control-plane operations. Both are proven; the difference is whether you amortize migration risk continuously or batch it.

Attitude to global services: Google operates true global services but enforces synthetic failure discipline; AWS doctrine minimizes globality outright (regional independence, regional control planes); Meta is global-by-default at the product layer with region drain/failover; OCI forbids globality across realms entirely. No one disputes the risk — they dispute whether to tame or ban the global tier.
anti_patterns: Control plane on the request/recovery path: AWS REL11-BP04 explicitly forbids relying on control planes during recovery; routers must serve last-known-good. Any design where losing the placement/tenant-directory service stops traffic is rejected by all five.

Hidden dependencies on global services: Google's Global Chubby lesson — a too-reliable global service silently accumulates hard dependencies; they now deliberately take it down quarterly. Corollary anti-pattern: letting anything beyond routing/identity/aggregation become global.

Unbounded cell growth / untested cell limits: AWS calls out 'scaling cliffs' and unseen limits that only manifest at size; a cell whose maximum was never load-tested is not a cell, it's a future outage.

Shared state or synchronous dependencies between cells: AWS whitepaper — 'cells should not share state or components'; cross-cell calls reintroduce correlated failure and defeat the bulkhead. Cross-cell reporting belongs in a separate offline aggregation plane (Azure).
Single-stamp/single-cell deployments: Azure mandates ≥2 stamps from day one because one-instance topologies breed hard-coded assumptions that block later scale-out.

Hand-tuned heuristic placement at scale: Meta explicitly migrated Shard Manager from heuristics to constraint solvers for maintainability; humans assigning tenants to cells by spreadsheet does not survive growth.
Pure silo for everyone: SaaS Lens warns dedicated-stack-per-tenant forfeits SaaS economics (idle capacity, operational fan-out); silo is a tier, not the architecture.

Big-bang deployment across all cells/rings simultaneously: retired everywhere; Azure SDP, AWS wave deployment, Google canarying all exist to prevent the deployment from becoming the correlated failure cells were built to contain.
Throttling deep in the stack instead of at admission: AWS fairness doctrine puts token buckets at the front door before expensive work; discovering overload at the database is too late.

Random/locality-blind tenant→infrastructure assignment: Meta found pure Social Hash (bucket-independent) insufficient and replaced it with connection-aware routing; assignment without overlap bounds (shuffle-shard property) lets one tenant's failure correlate across the fleet.
oyatie_prescriptions: Define the cell contract now (extends ADR-0341/0348): a cell = one Talos-imaged Kubernetes cluster + its own datastores/queues/per-cell observability stack, zero shared state with sibling cells. Cluster-per-cell, not namespace-per-cell — the k8s control plane is itself a blast-radius boundary (Borg-cell analogy). Cap cell size with a published limit in three units (TPS, tenant count, storage GB) and add a buck2-built full-scale cell load test that runs before any limit change; never operate a cell above ~70% of tested max so failover headroom exists (AWS REL01-BP06 doctrine).

Build the cell router as the thinnest possible Rust/axum data-plane layer: tenant_id→cell route table compiled as a content-addressed artifact and shipped over the ADR-0516..0535 delivery fabric, loaded into router memory, served from last-known-good when the control plane is unreachable (AWS S3-route-cache pattern). No per-request directory lookups against a live database (reject the Azure APIM/Cosmos smart-gateway shape — it violates static stability). Also expose per-cell DNS endpoints (cell-N.region.oyatie.cloud) for break-glass direct addressing.

Stand up a placement service in the control plane as a first-class product: inputs = per-cell capacity/used/quota, tenant size trajectory, cost-of-move, affinity; start with deterministic bin-packing + headroom rules, design the interface so a constraint solver (Meta Shard Manager model) can replace the heuristic later without API change. Control plane is CP and allowed to fail; encode the CP/AP split as a buck2 dependency lint: data-plane targets may not link control-plane clients on the request path.

Implement tenant migration as a day-one state machine, because single-tenant→multi-tenant is itself one giant migration: clone → flip-authoritative → redirect → forget, with dual-mapping/cross-cell redirects during transition and graceful in-flight request forwarding (Shard Manager handover). Rehearse migrations weekly against synthetic tenants in production cells; a migration path that only runs during emergencies does not exist.

Adopt the bridge isolation model with tier-driven placement: pooled cells with row-level tenancy for standard tiers, dedicated silo cells for premium/regulated/whale tenants (a tenant that dominates a cell gets evicted to its own cell — AWS rule). Inside pooled cells, enforce tenancy with Cedar (ADR-0243): every policy carries tenant_id on principal AND resource, and the axum extractor injects the authenticated tenant context so a missing tenant scope is a type error, not a code-review hope — this is the Cedar equivalent of AWS's per-tenant IAM scoping.

Shuffle-shard pooled cells internally: assign each tenant a k-of-n subset of workers/queues per cell and enforce the Route 53 overlap bound (no two tenants share more than f workers; with n=8,k=2 you already get 28 virtual shards). This contains poison-pill requests and gives single-tenant blast-radius on pooled infra; keep assignment static and auditable (AWS) rather than solver-churned until scale forces otherwise.

Admission control at the front door, per tenant, before any expensive work: hierarchical composed token buckets in axum middleware (low-rate/high-burst + high-rate/low-burst to bound burst rate), quotas keyed to tenant tier and raised with organic growth, heavy-hitter/top-talker telemetry into cloud/observability/. Quotas are part of the tenant contract and a billing input, not an ops tweak.

Ratify a 'thin global layer' allowlist ADR: ONLY (a) cell routing + tenant directory, (b) IdP token issuance (regionally replicated, tokens verifiable per-cell offline so cells authenticate during IdP outage), (c) billing/analytics aggregation off the request path. Everything else is per-cell. Enforce with a scheduled Chubby-style gameday: synthetically black-hole each global service quarterly and fail the SLO gate (ADR-0130 substrate) of any service that breaks — this converts the anti-pattern check into CI.

Deployment = waves over cells, wired into oya-ci/Tide (ADR-0513): one-box canary cell → 1 cell → 10% → 25% → 100% with bake time and automated per-cell SLO health gates (Azure SDP/Gandalf model); cells must tolerate version skew (n/n-1) since waves imply heterogeneity. The cell router is deployed on its own, slower, more conservative wave than cells.

Per-tenant cost attribution from the first multi-tenant request: every metric/log/trace/storage op tagged tenant_id + cell_id + tier in the observability substrate; compute cost-per-tenant and per-tier margin continuously (SaaS Lens COST_1/COST_2) and feed it back into placement (co-tenancy decisions) and pricing. Retrofitting attribution later is what every hyperscaler blog warns about.

Build Defcon-style degraded mode into the service framework: a per-cell, locally-evaluated feature-criticality knob system (axum layer + config artifact via the delivery fabric, no global flag service on the request path), with knobs exercised regularly in production so their capacity savings are measured, not assumed. Pair with static stability: every data-plane service must define and test its behavior under 'control plane gone, config stale'.

Alarm on cells, aggregate elsewhere: per-cell SLOs (the {oya,cloud}/<service>/slos/*.openslo.yaml mandate maps cleanly — add cell as a label dimension), worst-cell dashboards for blast-radius verification, and a separate analytics plane for cross-cell/cross-tenant rollups. Cross-cell queries on the request path are forbidden by the cell contract.

Data partitioning: database-per-cell with pooled tenant_id row-level schema inside each cell; avoid schema-per-tenant (migration fan-out grows O(tenants), every hyperscaler's pooled tier avoids it); whales get dedicated cells, not special schemas. Design tenant data export/import (the migration clone step) as a supported product capability — it doubles as your enterprise data-residency and realm story (OCI realms show single-tenant 'whole-substrate' deployments are a sellable top tier for an owned-stack vendor like Oyatie).

research.domain: Unified console / frontend shell hosting many product modules (hyperscaler cloud-console architecture)

per_company.approach: AWS Management Console = federation of independently deployed per-service console SPAs composed under a platform-owned shell ('Unified Navigation'). Shell owns: unified search (launched Dec 2020 — searches services, features, Marketplace, docs without leaving console), notifications center (AWS User Notifications + AWS Health), CloudShell entry, account/billing menu, region picker, settings, and customizable Console Home widgets (2022: Recently Visited, Health, announcements, blogs). Auth is shell-owned via AWS Sign-In (signin.aws.amazon.com); federated console sessions up to 12h; Jan 2025 multi-session lets one browser hold up to 5 simultaneous identities (root/IAM/federated), each session isolated per tab — tenant switching by parallel sessions, not mutable global context. Resilience: regional console endpoints https://{region}.console.aws.amazon.com documented in AWS General Reference, so a console fault domain follows the region. Design-system governance: Cloudscape, created 2016 explicitly to unify inconsistent AWS web-app UX, open-sourced July 2022 (Apache 2.0, cloudscape-design org): 60+ components, 30+ pattern guidelines, theming, dark mode, content-density modes, semantic markup + ARIA built into components, bidirectionality (RTL) as a stated core principle. Cloudscape is the de facto shell↔module visual contract; AWS's own prescriptive guidance for shells recommends manifest-based client-side discovery (name/URL/version/fallback per micro-frontend) — notably the official micro-frontend guidance recommends web components or module federation, NOT iframes.

Azure Portal ('Ibiza', GA 2015) is the most explicit extension-model console: shell + separately deployed 'extensions', each loaded into a hidden sandboxed iframe on its own origin; extension Blades/Parts follow MVVM (Knockout.js ViewModels), and UI is projected into the shell DOM via object-remoting — the SDK diffs Knockout observables and ships diff-grams over postMessage between the iframe and shell copies of the ViewModel. Documented rationale for isolation: (1) security — extension HTTP access restricted to specific origins, (2) reliability — extension bugs have bounded blast radius, (3) scale — extension JS can be unloaded. History: 2013 browsers couldn't handle one visible iframe per tile, hence hidden-iframe remoting; circa 2018 browsers scaled better and UX pivoted to full-screen blades, so Ibiza added FrameBlade (visible iframe, extension owns DOM directly — but is then 'fully responsible for accessibility, theming, consistency') and later a declarative JSON extension model to cut SDK burden. Token contract: shell acquires Entra tokens; extension ajax() auto-attaches tokens, getAuthorizationToken() for manual attach; third-party extensions receive an ENCRYPTED token only ARM can decrypt, so they cannot call alternate resources — first-party extensions get broader scopes. Operations: Ibiza team runs a common global extension hosting service (safe-deployment, region-aware version resolution) plus built-in A/B flighting via ExP. Hard performance admission bar: BladeFullReady < 4s at p80 and < 8s at p95 required before PROD enablement, ≥100 loads for valid signal, and a portfolio-level Weighted Experience Score (WxP) must exceed 80. Design language: Fluent UI.

Google Cloud Console is a monorepo (google3) Angular SPA — Angular is confirmed for Cloud Console, Firebase Console, parts of Gmail; Google's monorepo holds ~4,500 Angular apps, some with millions of LOC. Per Doug Parker (Angular team, Angular Meetup Graz / Ng-News 26/04): Cloud Console previously ran 'a huge micro frontend architecture using an iFrame approach, which is not used anymore'; the replacement does micro-frontends in COMPLETE isolation — nothing shared at all (explicit collision-avoidance), cross-MFE communication via Protocol Buffers as a messaging contract rather than shared code, multi-framework capable, framed as 'a contract between apps — an interface that needs to be implemented'; no plan to open-source it. Composition leans on monorepo build-time integration rather than runtime federation. Parker's caveats: only adopt MFEs when build-time alternatives won't suffice; hard UX requirements make MFEs difficult; don't use them to dodge inter-team communication. Shell owns project/organization picker (tenant context), global search, Cloud Shell. Design governance: Material Design across consoles. Performance trajectory: the Angular+Wiz merger (announced 2024) imports Wiz's latency discipline (used by Search, Photos, Payments) into the framework Cloud Console sits on.

No public cloud; the equivalents are Comet (the React+Relay+GraphQL rewrite of facebook.com, 2020) as app-shell infrastructure and a federated design-system estate for internal/business tools. Comet facts: atomic CSS generated at build time cut homepage CSS ~80% (old site shipped 400+KB compressed CSS with ~10% used initially); CSS variables for runtime theming/dark mode; three-tier code splitting (Tier 1 ~50KB layout/skeleton, Tier 2 ~150KB above-fold interactive, Tier 3 ~300KB deferred logging/subscriptions); EntryPoints parallelize code+data download via route maps and hover/focus prefetch; GraphQL @stream/@defer for incremental data; per-product JavaScript byte budgets enforced on merge requests with dependency-graph tooling and historical dashboards. Design-system governance: ~20 product design systems tied together by a top-level Cross Meta Design System; largest are Blueprint (Facebook) and Geodesic (business/ads tools); each system ships docs (internal Dimsum site), Figma libraries, React + native components, and support groups, with dedicated designer+engineer staffing per system. Internal-tools lineage: 2010 internal dashboards framework let non-engineers compose widget pages; Phabricator originated as FB's internal tool suite; >100,000 React components dogfooded across production and internal tools — internal surfaces ride the same React infra as product.

OCI Console is React/TypeScript/Redux (Oracle Cloud Infrastructure careers: 'improving user experience by building rich UIs using TypeScript, React, and Redux') — NOT Oracle JET for the OCI console proper; JET (MVVM toolkit, open source) and the Redwood design system are used across Oracle's Fusion/SaaS cloud applications. The distinctive trait is realm/region-aware shell topology: realms (commercial OC1, gov/defense realms) have fully separate console domains — e.g., console.us-gov-ashburn-1.oraclegovcloud.com, console.us-langley-1.oraclegovcloud.com — so sovereignty isolation extends to the console plane itself; within the commercial realm, region-specific URLs (console.us-ashburn-1.oraclecloud.com) are being DEPRECATED in favor of a single global entry cloud.oracle.com with in-shell region switching. Shell owns tenancy + compartment context (compartment tree is the cross-service authorization scoping UI), region switcher, language switching (documented i18n), configurable session timeout, billing/cost widgets, and contextually aware help.

convergent_patterns: Platform-owned thin shell for ALL cross-cutting chrome — every one of the five puts global navigation, unified search, notifications, identity/session, tenant/region context switching, settings, and theming in a single platform team's shell; product modules ship content panes only and are forbidden from re-implementing chrome (AWS Unified Navigation docs, Azure Ibiza shell, GCP top bar/project picker, OCI region+compartment shell, Meta Comet app shell).

One mandated design system owned by a dedicated team as the de facto shell↔module contract: Cloudscape (AWS, created 2016 to fix per-service UX fragmentation), Fluent (Azure), Material (Google), Cross-Meta-governed family of ~20 systems (Meta), Redwood/JET + console component library (Oracle). All bake accessibility semantics, theming/dark mode, and density into components so module teams get compliance 'for free'; teams escaping the system (Azure FrameBlade) explicitly inherit full responsibility for a11y/theming/consistency — the documented cost of opting out.

Independent module deployment with shell-mediated composition and safe rollout: Azure's hosting service does region-aware version resolution + ExP flighting; AWS service consoles deploy independently behind manifest/URL composition with regional endpoints; Google composes from the monorepo at build time; Meta enforces per-product budgets at merge. In all cases module teams ship on their own cadence WITHOUT a coordinated shell release.

Shell-owned token brokerage — modules never touch raw credentials: Azure documents it hardest (portal acquires Entra tokens, ajax() auto-attaches, third-party extensions get tokens encrypted such that only ARM can decrypt them); AWS Sign-In owns the session and federated token minting; Google/Meta single-session SPA with platform auth. Scoped, audience-restricted token handoff from shell to module is the universal pattern.

Percentile-based performance admission gates, not aspirations: Azure refuses PROD enablement until BladeFullReady < 4s p80 / < 8s p95 with ≥100-load signal and portfolio WxP > 80; Meta enforces per-product JS byte budgets on merge requests with dashboards; Google's whole Wiz merger is latency-driven; Comet's tiered (50/150/300KB) loading is a budget architecture. Performance is a GATE owned by the platform, measured per module, rolled up to a portfolio score.

Convergence AWAY from runtime iframe composition for first-party modules: Google retired its iframe MFE architecture for Cloud Console; Azure moved from hidden-iframe Knockout remoting toward full-screen FrameBlades + declarative models; AWS's own guidance recommends web components/module federation and omits iframes entirely; Meta never used them. Iframes survive only where genuinely untrusted third-party extensibility demands an origin sandbox (Azure's documented security/reliability/scale rationale).

Region/realm-aware console serving as a fault-isolation and sovereignty boundary: AWS regional console endpoints ({region}.console.aws.amazon.com), OCI realm-separated console domains (oraclegovcloud.com vs oraclecloud.com) with a global entry point routing into regions, Azure hosting service loading extension versions by accessing region. The console plane inherits the same partitioning discipline as the data plane.

Contract-first module integration: Azure's Blade/Part SDK contract, Google's 'an interface that needs to be implemented' + protobuf messaging with ZERO shared dependencies, AWS's manifest (name/URL/version/fallback) discovery — composition is governed by a versioned, typed contract, never by shared mutable code.
divergences: Isolation technology — driven by trust model and repo topology: Azure treats modules as semi-trusted separately-deployed extensions (third-party extensibility is a product requirement) → runtime iframe sandbox + postMessage RPC; Google has all-first-party monorepo modules → build-time composition, complete dependency isolation, protobuf contracts, no iframes; AWS sits between → independently deployed per-service SPAs unified by URL routing + shared design system; Meta is the extreme trusted end → one coherent app framework (Comet) shared outright.

Dependency-sharing philosophy is directly contradictory: Google shares NOTHING between micro-frontends (explicit collision-avoidance policy, services replaced by protobuf messaging); AWS shares Cloudscape component code across all consoles; Meta shares the entire framework and 100k+ components. The deciding variable is whether modules version-skew independently at runtime (Google/Azure: yes → share nothing) or are built atomically from one monorepo commit (Meta: safe to share everything).

Framework bets: Angular (Google, ~4,500 internal apps), React (AWS Cloudscape, Meta, OCI Console), Knockout.js→TypeScript declarative JSON (Azure portal SDK — widely seen as legacy drag and the reason for the FrameBlade/declarative escape hatches), JET/Preact toolkit for Oracle's Fusion side. No convergence on framework; total convergence on 'one framework per console, mandated'.

Tenant-context switching model: AWS chose parallel isolated sessions (multi-session, up to 5 identities, one per tab, opt-in 2025) — eliminating mutable-global-context bugs; Azure/Google/OCI use in-shell mutable context switches (directory, project/org, region+compartment). AWS's choice trades memory/complexity for correctness under cross-account comparison workflows.

Extensibility ambition: Azure designed for third-party extension authorship from day one (hence the heavyweight sandbox + SDK + hosting service + performance bar bureaucracy); Google/Meta explicitly keep composition internal-only and will not open-source it; AWS exposes only the design system (Cloudscape), not the shell contract. The cost of Azure's openness is the most complex SDK contract in the industry; the benefit is hundreds of teams shipping on one governance rail.
anti_patterns: Runtime iframe micro-frontends for first-party modules — Google built Cloud Console this way and RETIRED it ('not used anymore' per Angular team); Azure's hidden-iframe + Knockout object-remoting is acknowledged legacy (2013 browser constraint) that they've been escaping since ~2018 via FrameBlades and declarative models.

Shared mutable dependencies across independently deployed frontend modules — Google's replacement architecture 'does not share anything at all' specifically to avoid version-collision hell; communication moved to protobuf message contracts.

Adopting micro-frontends as an org-chart workaround — Google explicitly warns against using MFEs 'primarily to reduce inter-team communication' or when build-time improvements would suffice, and notes hard UX consistency requirements make MFEs difficult.

Monolithic asset shipping — Meta's pre-Comet site shipped 400+KB compressed CSS with ~10% used on initial render; replaced by build-time atomic CSS (80% reduction) and tiered code splitting. Unbudgeted bundles are treated as regressions blocked at merge time.

Per-service bespoke UI design — the pre-2016 AWS console's fragmented per-team UX is exactly what Cloudscape was created to eliminate; no hyperscaler lets module teams pick their own component library.

Letting modules handle credentials — Azure's contract makes it structurally impossible for third-party extensions to use tokens against non-ARM audiences (encrypted tokens); no console hands refresh credentials to modules.

Region-specific console URLs as the user-facing entry (commercial realm) — OCI is deprecating console.<region>.oraclecloud.com bookmarks in favor of one global entry with in-shell region routing; regional endpoints remain as resilience/ops surfaces (AWS keeps them documented for fault isolation), not as primary UX.

Escaping the design system without absorbing its obligations — Azure documents that FrameBlade authors become 'fully responsible for accessibility, theming, consistency'; the platform makes opt-out expensive and visible rather than banning it.
oyatie_prescriptions: Build exactly one platform-owned shell service (e.g., oya/console-shell) that owns ALL chrome: global nav, unified search, notification center, tenant/region/cell context, settings, theming bootstrap, telemetry init, feature-flag bootstrap, and token brokerage. Product modules register content panes via a versioned manifest; they are contractually forbidden from re-implementing chrome. This is the single strongest 5/5 convergent signal.

Choose Google-style build-time composition from the buck2 monorepo for first-party modules — NOT runtime iframes, NOT webpack module federation. Each console module is an independent buck2 target emitting a content-addressed bundle (ADR-0516..0535 delivery fabric is a perfect fit); the shell composes via a route-registration manifest (name, route, bundle digest, version, fallback — mirroring AWS's manifest schema). Atomic monorepo commits make Meta-style full sharing of the design system safe; Google's 'share nothing at runtime' rule applies only if you later allow out-of-band module deploys.

Define the shell↔module contract as a versioned, typed schema checked into the monorepo (Oyatie's IDL or serde-typed events): (1) route registration + deep-link format carrying tenant+region+cell context, (2) typed event bus for cross-module messaging (Google's protobuf-contract pattern — no shared singletons), (3) theming via CSS custom properties (Meta pattern: runtime dark mode with no reload), (4) telemetry context propagation injected by the shell, (5) feature-flag evaluation handed down, never fetched ad hoc by modules.

Make the shell the sole token broker, enforced with Cedar (ADR-0243): the shell holds the session, mints short-lived audience-scoped tokens per module request, and Cedar policies bind token audience to module identity — reproducing Azure's strongest documented control (third-party tokens encrypted so only ARM can use them). Modules MUST be structurally unable to call APIs outside their declared audience. This is also the pre-built rail for future third-party extensions.

Reserve an Azure-style sandboxed-iframe extension lane as the FUTURE third-party mechanism only (separate origin, postMessage RPC, scoped encrypted tokens, its own performance bar) — do not pay its complexity tax for first-party modules. Azure proves the sandbox is for trust boundaries, not for team boundaries.

Stand up the Oyatie design system as a first-class product with a dedicated owner from day one (Cloudscape model: components + pattern guidelines + demos): WCAG 2.1 AA semantics, keyboard nav, ARIA, dark mode, density modes, and RTL/bidirectionality built into components; i18n string externalization mandatory. Treat 'used the design system' as a merge-gate, and make opt-outs (custom canvases) explicitly inherit full a11y/theming responsibility like Azure FrameBlades.

Adopt Azure's admission bar verbatim as an oya-ci promotion gate, wired into ADR-0130 SLO-gated promotion: module FullReady < 4s at p80 AND < 8s at p95 (≥100-load signal) authored as {oya,cloud}/<service>/slos/*.openslo.yaml before any console module promotes past dev; compute a portfolio Weighted Experience Score (>80) across all modules for ops review. Add Meta-style per-module JS/CSS byte budgets enforced on every PR with trend dashboards — budgets are CI gates, not guidelines.

Implement Comet-style tiered loading in the shell: Tier-1 shell skeleton (~50KB-class), Tier-2 above-fold module interactivity, Tier-3 deferred telemetry/subscriptions; route-manifest-driven prefetch on hover/focus; parallelize module code + data fetch (EntryPoints pattern) — the shell, not modules, owns this orchestration.

Serve the console cell/region-aware per ADR-0341/0348: console bundles replicated per cell via the content-addressed delivery fabric, console session pinned to the tenant's home cell, shuffle-sharded static serving; keep ONE global entry domain that routes into the home cell (OCI cloud.oracle.com model) and reserve hard realm-style console-domain separation for sovereign/regulated single-tenant enclaves. Rollback = manifest pointer flip per cell (content-addressing makes this O(1)).

For the single-tenant→multi-tenant path, ship AWS-style multi-session from the start: each tenant/role session is an isolated, immutable context (one per tab, cap ~5) rather than a mutable global switcher — this eliminates the entire cross-tenant context-bleed bug class before it exists, which matters double for an owned-IdP product where the console is also the IdP's showcase.

Safe deployment of modules copies Azure's hosting service: modules publish versioned bundles; the shell resolves version per cell/region with staged rollout + flighting (feature-flag substrate dogfooded); ≥100-load statistical gates before widening; instant rollback by manifest pointer. Never require a shell release to ship or roll back a module.

research.domain: Control plane architecture, uniform resource model (resource-provider contract, LRO/operation ledger, hierarchy, tagging, quota), and metering→billing pipeline — across AWS, Google, Azure, OCI, and Meta internal

per_company.approach: Resource model: ARN (arn:partition:service:region:account:resource) as universal typed ID; the ACCOUNT is the hardest isolation boundary (no sub-account resource groups), composed via Organizations (management account, OUs, SCPs, tag policies, consolidated billing). Uniform CRUD: Cloud Control API (2021) exposes one CRUDL surface over the CloudFormation Registry — each resource type is a JSON Schema document (properties + handlers + per-handler IAM permissions); handlers must pass a published contract-test suite ('uniform set of behaviors... prevents creation of unintended or duplicate resources'); several hundred AWS types + third-party types onboard via the same contract; Terraform AWSCC provider is auto-generated from these schemas. LRO: async-by-default — mutations return ProgressEvent + RequestToken, polled via GetResourceRequestStatus, cancellable via CancelResourceRequest; create/update/delete take a client-token (UUID) idempotency parameter; one in-flight operation per resource; NO automatic rollback on partial failure. Control-plane doctrine (Builders' Library): strict control/data plane split, static stability (data plane runs on last-known config through control-plane outage), 'rely on data plane not control plane during recovery' (REL11-BP04); Physalia (NSDI'20) cellizes EBS control-plane config state into millions of tiny Paxos cells to minimize blast radius — keys only need availability at the client + 2 replicas, sidestepping CAP globally. Quota: Service Quotas service = central registry of default vs applied quotas, usage via CloudWatch AWS/Usage metrics (CallCount/ResourceCount per minute), Automatic Management auto-files increase requests at utilization thresholds. Metering: re:Invent ARC308 — internal metering pipeline at ~100M records/sec ingestion built on principles of 100% accuracy, once-and-only-once, idempotent processing, loose coupling (Kinesis/S3/EMR); ex-metering-team leadership cites ~2B events/sec on one platform today; Marketplace contract: hourly MeterUsage per dimension per customer, records rejected if >6h late (explicit lateness window); billing data productized as CUR → Data Exports with FOCUS 1.0 GA (Nov 2024: ListCost/ContractedCost/BilledCost/EffectiveCost). Versioning: Vogels' 'APIs are forever — never break backward compatibility'; 2006 S3 API calls still served. Tagging: tags double as cost-allocation dimensions (activated in billing) and ABAC attributes in IAM condition keys, governed org-wide by tag policies + SCP enforcement at create time.

Hierarchy: organization → folders → projects → resources; every resource has exactly one parent; IAM + org policies inherit down; the project is simultaneously the isolation, quota, billing, and API-enablement unit. API uniformity is enforced by published law: the AIP corpus (google.aip.dev) — AIP-122 hierarchical resource names ('tenants/{t}/things/{id}', user-settable IDs), standard methods only, AIP-151 LROs (every slow mutation returns google.longrunning.Operation; one uniform Operations service per API with Get/List/Cancel; metadata carries progress; errors as google.rpc.Status; ~30-day operation expiry), AIP-155 request_id idempotency (UUID4, duplicate returns the prior response), AIP-128 declarative-friendly resources (strongly consistent standard methods, output-only 'reconciling' + etag fields, no output-only fields in spec, LRO updates that may preempt prior ops marking them ABORTED — designed so Terraform/KRM tooling works generically), AIP-180/181/185 versioning (major-version-only — v1 never v1.4.2; removal of any component within a major version is forbidden). The shared serving layer is productized as Service Infrastructure: Service Management (config), Service Control (ADMISSION CONTROL on every request — API key, quota allocateQuota, billing checks — and TELEMETRY REPORTING on every response feeding Cloud Billing/Monitoring; designed for millions of producers/consumers; 6M quota units/min/producer cap; rate quotas per-minute-per-consumer-project), Service Usage (consumer enable/disable + quota overrides). State: control planes are Spanner-backed (GKE stores cluster state in Spanner behind an etcd API shim; Spanner/Colossus/Borg/Chubby underpin customer-facing services). Metering exemplar: Mesa (VLDB'14) — geo-replicated, near-real-time measurement warehouse for the ads/billing pipeline: petabytes, millions of row-updates/sec, billions of queries fetching trillions of rows/day, consistent repeatable query answers across full-datacenter failover via multi-versioned batched atomic updates. Tags vs labels split: governed Resource Manager Tags (inherit down hierarchy, drive IAM Conditions + org-policy enforcement) are deliberately separate from labels (billing annotations only, cannot gate policy). IaC: Deployment Manager (bespoke YAML/Jinja DSL) deprecated, EOL 2026-03-31, replaced by Infrastructure Manager = managed Terraform + Config Connector (KRM).

ARM is a mandatory front-door proxy: ALL management requests flow through Azure Resource Manager, which authenticates/authorizes once, then forwards to resource providers that must implement the published Resource Provider Contract (RPC): idempotent PUT/GET/PATCH/DELETE with standardized headers, client timeouts, throttling and response-size rules; provisioningState with exactly three terminal states (Succeeded/Failed/Canceled); two uniform async patterns — 201+provisioningState polling on the resource, or 202+Location / Azure-AsyncOperation header polling; tracked vs proxy-only resource classification; subscription-lifecycle APIs every provider must honor. Hierarchy: management groups (10,000 per directory, 6 levels) → subscriptions → resource groups (every resource lives in exactly one RG) → resources; Azure Policy + RBAC assignments cascade down by inheritance and are additive (no child-scope deny of parent grants); policy enforces tag compliance because tags explicitly do NOT inherit from subscription/RG to resources (acknowledged wart, patched via built-in tag-inheritance policies). API versioning: every request carries a date-stamped api-version pinned per provider; old api-versions stay served. Billing: every service emits usage against METER IDs into the Commerce data pipeline on per-service cadences; a central rating system applies the customer price sheet producing 'rated usage' (price+quantity per record); visibility latency 8–24h (EA/MCA), up to 72h (PAYG); Cost Management exports now ship native FOCUS-format datasets combining actual+amortized cost. IaC is native: ARM templates/Bicep deploy declaratively against the same control plane (what-if, deployment stacks). Historical: the pre-ARM classic Azure Service Management (ASM) model — per-service, non-uniform, no RGs/RBAC granularity — was wholesale retired in favor of ARM.

Hierarchy: tenancy → nested compartments; every resource lives in exactly one compartment; compartments are the policy, quota, AND cost boundary; OCIDs are the universal typed resource IDs. LRO: uniform Work Requests pattern — async mutations return opc-work-request-id header; each work request is itself a resource with an OCID, states ACCEPTED/IN_PROGRESS/SUCCEEDED/FAILED, percent-complete, a list of affected resources, plus ListWorkRequestErrors/ListWorkRequestLogs; sync validation errors return 4xx immediately while async failures land in the work request; 50+ services participate, though some expose service-specific work-request endpoints rather than the unified API (uniformity is imperfect); general work requests retained ~12 hours. Quota: distinctive declarative quota-policy language layered over service limits — statements like 'set compute-core quota ... to N in compartment X', with three verbs set/unset/zero ('zero' removes access entirely), written in the same style as IAM policy — quota-as-policy-language. Tagging: tag namespaces + defined tags (schema'd, permission-controlled) vs free-form tags; tag defaults auto-apply at create time per compartment; cost-tracking tags (max 10 per tenancy) flow into the billing system and statements; tags usable in IAM policy conditions. Billing: cost and usage reports; FOCUS-format billing data adopter alongside AWS/Azure/GCP.

No external billing — capacity is the internal currency and the 'billing' system is a reservation/solver economy. Twine (OSDI'20): single unified cluster manager over one shared fleet of millions of machines (rejected per-team clusters). RAS (SOSP'21): Resource Allowance System — capacity abstraction = 'reservation' (a dynamically maintained set of servers forming a logical cluster); a mixed-integer-programming solver continuously re-optimizes server→reservation assignment OFF the critical path while Twine does real-time container placement WITHIN reservations; failure + maintenance buffers are embedded in reservations; SLO-guaranteed capacity. Extended globally by Global Reservations Service + Regional Fluidity, which place services across regions from declared intent ('viewing the world as a computer'). Deployment/config control plane: Conveyor (OSDI'23) — ONE deployment tool, 30,000+ pipelines covering ~97% of services, driving Twine for binaries and Configerator (config-as-code with a data-distribution tree + Owl P2P delivery) for configs/ML models; 55% of container services do full continuous deployment. Control-plane storage: Delos (OSDI'20) — fully replicated ACID, strictly serializable store purpose-built for control-plane state with MINIMAL dependencies (solves the bootstrap problem: it must not depend on systems whose config it stores); virtual consensus (VirtualLog over swappable Loglets) enables in-place consensus-protocol upgrades; 1.8B transactions/day; backs Twine's Resource Broker (server fleet metadata), deployed as many small 5–9 machine cells per fleet fraction. Chargeback is capacity-attribution by reservation/team rather than invoices.

convergent_patterns: ONE resource-provider contract that every service must implement, enforced by machine-checkable contract tests against a typed resource schema: AWS CloudFormation/Cloud Control handler contract (JSON Schema + CRUDL handlers + contract-test suite), Azure ARM RPC (mandatory for onboarding as a provider), Google AIP standard methods + api-linter, OCI resource/work-request conventions. The platform team owns the gateway and the contract; service teams only implement handlers. AWS proves retrofit is possible but expensive — Google/Azure prove enforcing it from day one is cheaper.

Async-by-default mutations returning a FIRST-CLASS OPERATION RESOURCE with uniform polling, terminal states, structured errors, and documented retention: google.longrunning.Operation (AIP-151, ~30-day expiry, uniform Operations service), AWS ProgressEvent/RequestToken + GetResourceRequestStatus, ARM provisioningState (Succeeded/Failed/Canceled) + Azure-AsyncOperation/Location headers, OCI work requests (OCID, affected-resources list, error/log sub-collections). Never block an HTTP request on provisioning.

Client-supplied UUID idempotency token on every mutating call, with duplicate detection returning the previously successful response: AWS client-token, Google AIP-155 request_id (UUID4), ARM idempotent PUT semantics, OCI opc-retry-token. All five treat exactly-once-from-the-client's-view as a control-plane invariant.

A single hierarchical resource-container tree that is simultaneously the attach point for identity/policy, quota, AND cost aggregation, with inheritance flowing down: Organizations→OUs→accounts (AWS), org→folders→projects (Google), management groups→subscriptions→resource groups (Azure), tenancy→nested compartments (OCI). Every resource has exactly one parent.

Governed tags as a cross-cutting dimension serving BOTH authorization (ABAC/IAM conditions) and cost allocation, with central schema governance: AWS tag policies + SCP enforcement + cost-allocation activation, GCP Resource Manager Tags (inherit, gate IAM + org policy) deliberately split from labels, OCI defined-tag namespaces + cost-tracking tags + tag defaults, Azure Policy-enforced tags grouping billing data. All four converged on schema'd/governed tags over free-form strings.

Control plane / data plane separation with STATIC STABILITY: the data plane must keep serving from last-known-good state through a total control-plane outage, and recovery paths must not depend on the control plane (AWS Builders' Library + REL11-BP04; Google's Service Infrastructure management/control/data plane split; Meta's Configerator distribution trees serving cached configs; Talos-relevant). Control-plane state lives in small, strongly consistent, blast-radius-bounded stores: Physalia cells (AWS EBS), Spanner (Google), Delos cells with zero-dependency bootstrap (Meta).

Metering separated from rating separated from invoicing, as an append-only exactly-once event pipeline: raw usage events (tenant, meter, quantity, timestamp, dedup key) → dedup/aggregate → rate against price sheet → invoice. AWS internal metering principles: 100% accuracy, once-and-only-once, idempotent, horizontally scalable; Azure Commerce pipeline with meter IDs and a distinct rating stage; Google Service Control telemetry feeding Cloud Billing, with Mesa-class warehousing for invoice-grade consistency. Explicit late-event windows (AWS Marketplace: 6 hours) and replayability are part of the contract.

FOCUS (FinOps Open Cost & Usage Specification) as the now-universal billing-data interchange format: AWS Data Exports FOCUS 1.0 GA, Azure Cost Management FOCUS exports, GCP and OCI FOCUS exports; FOCUS 1.2 (May 2025) adds SaaS/PaaS billing, invoice reconciliation, multi-currency — directly aimed at SaaS vendors like Oyatie.

No-breaking-changes API doctrine with major-version-only surfaces: Amazon 'APIs are forever' (2006 S3 calls still served), Google AIP-180/185 (no minor/patch versions exposed; removing any component within a major version is forbidden; stability levels alpha/beta/stable), Azure date-stamped api-versions served indefinitely. Compatibility is enforced by linters/contract diffs, not code review goodwill.

Declarative-IaC-friendliness as a control-plane API DESIGN CONSTRAINT, not a bolted-on tool: AIP-128 (strong consistency on standard methods, user-settable IDs, etag optimistic concurrency, reconciling field, no output-only spec fields), AWS resource schemas code-generating the Terraform AWSCC provider, ARM templates/Bicep operating natively against the provider contract. The resource schema is the single source from which IaC providers, SDKs, docs, and contract tests are generated. Read-back must equal write-in (no drift by construction).

Central quota service checked at ADMISSION, distinct from billing, with two quota kinds (rate per-time-window vs allocation/concurrent-count) and declarative override mechanisms: Google Service Control allocateQuota inline on every request; AWS Service Quotas registry + CloudWatch usage metrics + Automatic Management auto-increase; OCI declarative quota statements (set/unset/zero) per compartment; Azure quota APIs. Quota state is usage-metered, not guessed.
divergences: Grouping granularity vs isolation strength: AWS has NO sub-account resource grouping — the account itself is the (heavyweight, strongest) isolation cell, pushing customers to multi-account factories; Azure mandates lightweight resource groups (organizational, not a security boundary); GCP's project is a middle ground (isolation + quota + billing unit); OCI compartments are logical-only (resources stay put, policy moves). Disagreement is about whether the container is a hard tenancy boundary or a policy attachment point.

Where uniformity is enforced: Azure enforces via a mandatory runtime proxy (every call physically transits ARM); Google enforces via shared serving infrastructure (Service Control in the request path) PLUS design-time law (AIPs + api-linter); AWS enforced almost nothing for 15 years and then retrofitted uniformity as a wrapper layer (Cloud Control) over heterogeneous service APIs. Retrofit worked but only covers a subset of services and lags native APIs.

Cancellation semantics: Google mandates a uniform CancelOperation on every LRO service; AWS Cloud Control has CancelResourceRequest (in-flight only); ARM has no uniform cancel — only a Canceled terminal state; OCI cancel is per-service. Industry consensus exists on polling/terminal states, NOT on cancellation or rollback (AWS Cloud Control explicitly does not roll back partial failures, while CloudFormation-the-orchestrator does).

Tag inheritance: GCP Tags inherit down the resource hierarchy by design; Azure tags explicitly do NOT inherit (requires Azure Policy remediation); AWS tags never inherit; OCI splits the difference with create-time tag defaults per compartment. Reflects different views on whether tags are hierarchy metadata or per-resource facts.

Inline vs batch metering: Google meters inline at admission (Service Control telemetry on every response) giving near-real-time signal; AWS and Azure run batch pipelines with hours of latency (Azure 8–72h visibility; AWS hourly granularity, 6h late-window). Inline gives faster cost feedback and abuse cutoff; batch is simpler and decouples billing availability from serving.

Quota expression: OCI expresses quota as human-readable declarative policy statements; Google expresses quota as metrics with limits enforced by a quota server API; AWS treats quota as a registry + CloudWatch observability + ticketed/automated increases; Azure is fragmented per-service. No agreement on whether quota is policy, metric, or registry.

Meta diverges wholesale on the billing question: internally there is no money-denominated metering — capacity reservations with an MIP solver (RAS) plus global placement-by-intent replace quota+billing entirely, and chargeback is capacity attribution. The lesson for an internal substrate: reservations + solvers can replace price signals when there is one economic owner.

Bespoke IaC DSL vs ecosystem surrender: Azure doubled down on a first-party language (Bicep/ARM templates) tightly coupled to its provider contract; Google killed its first-party DSL (Deployment Manager) and surrendered to Terraform (Infrastructure Manager = managed Terraform); AWS keeps CloudFormation but co-invests in generating Terraform providers from its schemas. Strategy differs; the constant is that the resource schema/provider contract outlives any particular IaC syntax.
anti_patterns: Per-service, non-uniform control planes: Azure wholesale retired classic Azure Service Management (ASM) in favor of ARM; AWS's 15-year accumulation of heterogeneous service APIs forced the expensive Cloud Control retrofit; Google wrote the AIPs explicitly to prevent recurrence. Letting service #2 invent its own CRUD shape is the canonical sin.
Synchronous long-running mutations (blocking the request on provisioning): every provider moved to async-by-default with operation resources; ARM RPC and AIP-151 forbid it structurally.

Control-plane dependencies in data-plane recovery paths: AWS Well-Architected REL11-BP04 explicitly warns against it; static stability doctrine exists because control planes are statistically less available than data planes.

One big shared database for control-plane state: Physalia (AWS) explicitly rejects a monolithic store in favor of millions of per-volume cells to bound blast radius; Delos (Meta) runs as many small 5–9 node deployments and refuses dependencies on anything it stores config for (bootstrap rule); Google partitions Spanner-backed state regionally.

Bespoke IaC template DSLs as moats: Google Deployment Manager (YAML/Jinja/Python templates) deprecated with hard EOL 2026-03-31, migrated to Terraform-based Infrastructure Manager — a public retreat from proprietary IaC languages.

Using billing labels for authorization: GCP explicitly separated governed Tags (policy-capable, inherited, IAM-integrated) from labels because annotation metadata without governance cannot safely gate access.

Exposing minor/patch API versions or breaking changes within a major version: Google forbids v1.1-style versions outright (AIP-185); Amazon forbids breakage, period ('APIs are forever'); both treat deprecation-without-removal as the only path.

Trusting clients to retry without idempotency tokens: every provider mandates or strongly recommends client tokens because duplicate resource creation under retry is the most common control-plane corruption.
Fragmented per-team deployment/release tooling: Meta consolidated 30,000+ pipelines into one tool (Conveyor) covering ~97% of services; the prior per-team tool sprawl is the retired state.

Proprietary-only billing export schemas: all four clouds now ship FOCUS-format exports; AWS is actively migrating customers from CUR 1.0 to Data Exports/FOCUS — locking cost data in a bespoke schema is now an acknowledged liability.

Rolling back partial failures automatically at the resource-API layer: AWS Cloud Control deliberately does NOT roll back (rollback belongs to the orchestrator/IaC layer above); conflating the two creates unrecoverable states.
oyatie_prescriptions: Ratify the uniform resource-provider contract NOW, before more services land under {oya,cloud}/<service>/ (ADR-0131/0512 layout): a typed resource-schema registry (JSON Schema or protobuf in libs/, built by buck2) where every single-concern microservice (ADR-0132) implements CRUDL handlers; ship a shared Rust contract-test crate (mirroring the CloudFormation handler contract + ARM RPC rules: idempotent PUT, no duplicate creation, read-after-write equality, stable list pagination) and make it a buck2 test target gating cloud-ci promotion — same enforcement lane as the existing mandatory OpenSLO authoring rule.

Build ONE Operations service ('operation ledger') as a Rust crate + axum middleware before service #2 invents its own: every mutation returns operations/{id} with AIP-151 semantics — metadata (progress, reconciling), exactly three terminal states (Succeeded/Failed/Canceled), structured error payloads (google.rpc.Status-equivalent), CancelOperation where meaningful, ~30-day operation retention, and NO automatic rollback at this layer (rollback belongs to the IaC/orchestrator layer). Persist operations in the same cell-local store as the resource state so the ledger shards with cells (ADR-0341/0348).

Mandate client-supplied UUID idempotency tokens (AIP-155 style request_id) on all mutating endpoints, with a documented dedup retention window (7–30 days) and duplicate-returns-prior-response semantics; implement once in axum middleware backed by the operation ledger, never per-service.

Adopt AIP-122 hierarchical resource names with user-settable IDs as the universal ID scheme (tenants/{t}/compartments/{c}/.../resources/{id}, plus an ARN/OCID-style fully-qualified form). Critically for ADR-0348 autosharding: never encode cell, shard, or region into customer-visible IDs — IDs must survive tenant migration between cells.

Resource hierarchy: tenancy → nested compartments (OCI/GCP-folder style) with exactly-one-parent, and make this tree the SINGLE attach point for Cedar policy (ADR-0243 — Cedar's entity-hierarchy and parent-traversal model maps directly onto compartment inheritance), quota, and cost aggregation. This avoids AWS's no-grouping retrofit pain and is the cheapest decision to make early and the most expensive to change later.

Two annotation systems, never one (GCP's hard-learned lesson): governed 'tags' (schema'd namespaces à la OCI defined tags, bound to hierarchy nodes, inherited, referencable in Cedar conditions and quota/cost policy, with required-tag admission enforcement like AWS tag policies) and free-form 'labels' (reporting only, never policy-capable). Cost allocation fails silently without create-time tag enforcement.

Put an admission-control gateway in the request path (Google Service Control analog) as a shared axum layer: authn → Cedar authz → quota check → serve → emit one usage/telemetry record per response. This single chokepoint yields metering for free, keeps quota logic out of every service, and is the natural Cedar PDP integration point. Keep it cell-local so admission control shares the cell's fate, not a global dependency.

Quota as a first-class service with two kinds — rate quotas (per-window) and allocation quotas (counts) — expressed declaratively per compartment with OCI's three verbs (set/unset/zero; 'zero' = hard deny is essential for SaaS tenant suspension), backed by a central registry of defaults + per-tenant overrides, usage-metered, with automated increase workflows (AWS Automatic Management pattern). Evaluate at the admission gateway.

Metering pipeline as a separate append-only exactly-once system from day one: usage events (tenant, meter_id, quantity, timestamp, dedup_key) → dedup → windowed aggregation → rating (price sheet as versioned data, not code) → invoice; design for an explicit late-event window (AWS uses 6h), full replayability from the raw event log, and invoice-grade reconciliation invariants (sum(rated usage) == invoice, checked continuously). Emit FOCUS 1.2-conformant cost exports natively — all four clouds do, FOCUS 1.2 explicitly covers SaaS billing, and it is the standard enterprise FinOps ingestion path Oyatie's customers will demand.

Static stability as a tested invariant, not an aspiration: each cell's data plane (request serving + Cedar policy evaluation from cached/snapshotted policy + config) must keep serving through total control-plane outage; encode this as a cloud-ci chaos gate (kill control plane, assert data-plane SLOs hold). Recovery runbooks must use data-plane operations only (REL11-BP04).

Control-plane state store per cell, not global: small strongly consistent stores partitioned per cell (Physalia/Delos lesson), with Delos's bootstrap rule applied to Oyatie's dogfooded stack — the store holding IdP/policy/control config must not depend on the IdP/policy/control services it configures. Break the circular dependency explicitly in an ADR.

Versioning doctrine as a ratified ADR before the first external tenant: major-version-only API surfaces (v1, v1beta1), additive-only within a major version (AIP-180 rules), enforced mechanically — an api-linter-style checker plus golden-schema diff as buck2 targets in cloud-ci, failing the gate on any incompatible change. 'APIs are forever' is a governance artifact, not a culture hope.

IaC-friendliness as contract-test clauses (AIP-128): strong read-after-write consistency on standard methods, etag optimistic concurrency, reconciling field, no output-only fields in the spec block, idempotent create with user-settable IDs — so a Terraform provider AND a KRM-style operator (natural fit with the k8s+Talos substrate) are CODE-GENERATED from the same resource schemas via buck2, alongside Rust stubs, SDKs, docs, and contract tests. One schema, five generated artifacts.

For Oyatie's internal capacity economy (the Meta lane): treat cell/cluster capacity as reservations with embedded failure+maintenance buffers (RAS model) managed by the single deployment/promotion pipeline (ADR-0513 oya-ci, the Conveyor analog) — do not build per-service capacity tooling, and account internal usage by reservation attribution rather than synthetic dollars until multi-tenant billing externalizes real prices.
